cases.hp: Case summary: Jamal Wright reports escalating leg pain, numbness, and tightness under a cast after tibia fracture reduction, concerning for acute compartment syndrome. Focused exam shows tense anterior compartment, pain 10/10 despite opioid analgesia, paresthesia between the first and second toes, weight 76 kg, height 180 cm, and SpO2 99% on room air.
notes: Jamal says the pain feels like pressure and is worse than when the fracture happened. The nurse notes pain with passive toe extension and swelling at the cast edges.

Jamal reports new numbness between the first and second toes and says the pain medication did nothing. The nurse keeps the limb at heart level, avoids ice, and notifies the orthopedic provider immediately.
Neurovascular reassessment shows delayed capillary refill and a firm anterior compartment. Orders are given to loosen the cast, keep the client NPO, and prepare for possible fasciotomy.
The cast is bivalved by the provider and Jamal remains under close neurovascular monitoring. Pain is slightly improved but paresthesia persists.
Final reassessment shows improved capillary refill after cast release. Severe pain and paresthesia remain concerning, so urgent surgical evaluation continues.

diagnostics.result: Tense anterior compartment, pain with passive stretch, paresthesia in deep peroneal nerve distribution, capillary refill 4 seconds.

orders: Notify orthopedic surgeon STAT and prepare for possible fasciotomy
Keep limb at heart level and remove constrictive dressing/cast per provider direction
q1: Paresthesia between first and second toes
q2: row_a
Escalating pain out of proportion with passive stretch suggests compartment syndrome.
row_b
Palpable pulses would rule out compartment syndrome.
row_c
Paresthesia reflects nerve ischemia and is not a routine fracture symptom.
row_d
Elevating the limb high above the heart can worsen perfusion pressure.
hypotheses: Acute compartment syndrome threatening limb perfusion
solutions: Immediate: notify orthopedic surgeon and prepare for cast release/fasciotomy
Positioning: keep limb at heart level
Unsafe: apply ice and elevate high above heart
Preparation: keep NPO and maintain IV access
actions: Stop activity, keep the limb at heart level, and reassess neurovascular status
Notify the orthopedic provider STAT and prepare for cast loosening or bivalving
Keep Jamal NPO, maintain IV access, and prepare for possible fasciotomy
Continue neurovascular checks every 15 minutes and document changes
eval: eval_a
Capillary refill improves from 4 seconds to 2 seconds after cast release
eval_b
Pain decreases only from 10/10 to 8/10 and remains concerning
eval_c
Paresthesia persists and needs urgent follow-up
eval_d
SpO2 remains normal and does not indicate limb recovery

ehr.history_physical: Case summary: Jamal Wright reports escalating leg pain, numbness, and tightness under a cast after tibia fracture reduction, concerning for acute compartment syndrome. Focused exam shows tense anterior compartment, pain 10/10 despite opioid analgesia, paresthesia between the first and second toes, weight 76 kg, height 180 cm, and SpO2 99% on room air.

notes.note: Jamal says the pain feels like pressure and is worse than when the fracture happened. The nurse notes pain with passive toe extension and swelling at the cast edges.

Jamal reports new numbness between the first and second toes and says the pain medication did nothing. The nurse keeps the limb at heart level, avoids ice, and notifies the orthopedic provider immediately.
Neurovascular reassessment shows delayed capillary refill and a firm anterior compartment. Orders are given to loosen the cast, keep the client NPO, and prepare for possible fasciotomy.
The cast is bivalved by the provider and Jamal remains under close neurovascular monitoring. Pain is slightly improved but paresthesia persists.
Final reassessment shows improved capillary refill after cast release. Severe pain and paresthesia remain concerning, so urgent surgical evaluation continues.

diagnostics.result: Tense anterior compartment, pain with passive stretch, paresthesia in deep peroneal nerve distribution, capillary refill 4 seconds.

orders.order: Notify orthopedic surgeon STAT and prepare for possible fasciotomy
Keep limb at heart level and remove constrictive dressing/cast per provider direction
NPO and maintain IV access
Neurovascular checks every 15 minutes

cases.hp: Case summary: Grace Kim develops fever, chills, flank pain, hypotension, and dark urine shortly after packed red blood cell transfusion begins, concerning for acute hemolytic transfusion reaction. Focused exam shows rigors, anxiety, lumbar pain 8/10, dark red urine in Foley tubing, weight 68 kg, height 160 cm, and SpO2 94% on room air.
notes: Fifteen minutes after the PRBC transfusion starts, Grace reports chills and severe lower back pain. The nurse stops at the bedside and notes flushing, rigors, and new anxiety.

Grace becomes hypotensive and the Foley tubing contains dark red urine. The nurse stops the transfusion, maintains IV access with normal saline using new tubing, and calls the provider and blood bank.
Blood bank workup and hemolysis labs are ordered while Grace is monitored closely. The provider orders IV fluids, urine output monitoring, and return of the blood bag and tubing per policy.
Normal saline is infusing through new tubing and the blood product is sealed for return. Grace is less chilled but remains weak and worried.
Final reassessment shows blood pressure improving after fluids and no further transfusion exposure. Dark urine persists and creatinine begins to rise, so kidney injury surveillance continues.

diagnostics.result: Unit, tubing, compatibility tag, and patient identifiers collected for blood bank investigation.

orders: Stop transfusion immediately and do not restart blood product
Maintain IV access with 0.9% sodium chloride using new tubing
Notify provider and blood bank and return product/tubing per policy
Monitor vital signs, urine output, renal function, and DIC signs
mar: Acetaminophen only if prescribed after evaluation

io.intake: 50 mL PRBC before stopped; 500 mL normal saline

solutions: Safety: stop transfusion immediately and do not restart it
Access: keep IV open with normal saline using new tubing
Notify: provider and blood bank immediately
Unsafe: flush remaining blood through the line to keep it patent

actions: Maintain IV access with 0.9% sodium chloride using new tubing

cases.chief: Fever and sore throat after starting clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia

cases.pmh: Treatment-resistant schizophrenia, obesity, chronic constipation from antipsychotics
cases.social: Lives with sister who helps manage appointments and medication refills.
cases.hp: Case summary: Nadia Brooks reports fever and sore throat after starting clozapine, raising concern for serious neutropenia and infection risk. Focused exam shows mild pharyngeal erythema, fatigue, constipation, pain 3/10 throat soreness, weight 72 kg, height 167 cm, and SpO2 98% on room air.
notes: Nadia says her throat hurts and she almost skipped today’s blood test because she felt tired. The nurse notes that clozapine was started six weeks ago and verifies the most recent ANC result.
Nadia’s temperature increases and she asks if she can take the next clozapine dose to keep voices controlled. The nurse holds administration until the prescriber reviews the fever and ANC result.

Laboratory results show a critically low ANC and the prescriber is notified immediately. Orders include infection evaluation, medication hold pending provider decision, protective precautions as indicated, and patient teaching.

Nadia practices teach-back with her sister present and identifies fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, and flu-like symptoms as urgent reports. She also describes constipation prevention and avoiding abrupt medication changes without the prescriber.

Final reassessment shows Nadia understands infection warning signs and follow-up blood monitoring. She remains anxious about psychosis relapse, so psychiatric follow-up and safety planning are reinforced.

diagnostics.result: Mild erythema without airway compromise; blood cultures and viral testing ordered per provider.

orders: Hold clozapine pending urgent prescriber review for severe neutropenia
Initiate infection evaluation and neutropenic precautions as prescribed
Educate on ANC monitoring and urgent symptom reporting
Assess constipation, myocarditis symptoms, sedation, orthostatic hypotension, and seizure risk

io.output: Voids independently; no bowel movement for 2 days

cases.pmh: T4 complete spinal cord injury 4 months ago, neurogenic bladder with indwelling catheter, bowel program every other day
cases.social: Lives with spouse in an adapted apartment and is preparing for weekend pass.
cases.hp: Case summary: Ethan Moore has a T4 spinal cord injury and develops sudden pounding headache, flushing, sweating, and severe hypertension, consistent with autonomic dysreflexia. Focused exam shows flushed face, cool lower extremities, distended bladder, pain 9/10 headache, weight 74 kg, height 179 cm, and SpO2 98% on room air.
notes: Ethan says his head is pounding and he feels hot above the chest. The nurse notes facial flushing, sweating above the injury level, and a kinked urinary catheter tubing.
Blood pressure is far above Ethan’s baseline and his pulse is slower than usual. The nurse sits him upright, loosens clothing, checks catheter patency, and calls for assistance.

The catheter tubing is unkinked and 650 mL of urine drains rapidly into the bag. Provider orders continued blood pressure checks, trigger assessment, and short-acting antihypertensive medication if severe hypertension persists.
Ethan’s headache improves after bladder drainage and upright positioning. The nurse reviews home emergency steps with Ethan and his spouse using a wallet card and teach-back.
Final reassessment shows blood pressure near baseline and no recurrent headache. Ethan correctly describes first actions but needs reinforcement about when to seek emergency help.

diagnostics.result: Kinked catheter tubing with bladder distention; 650 mL drained after tubing corrected.

orders: Sit upright and remove tight clothing during suspected autonomic dysreflexia
Assess bladder catheter, bowel impaction risk, skin pressure, and other triggers
Monitor blood pressure every 2 to 5 minutes until stable
Administer short-acting antihypertensive per protocol if severe hypertension persists after trigger removal
mar: Topical lidocaine lubricant if catheter replacement required

io.output: 650 mL urine after catheter tubing unkinked

q1: Sudden pounding headache and facial flushing
Blood pressure 204/112 mm Hg with relative bradycardia
Kinked catheter tubing and bladder distention
q2: row_a
Autonomic dysreflexia is a medical emergency in injuries at or above T6.
row_b
Bladder distention is a common trigger and should be assessed immediately.
row_c
The client should be laid flat to improve brain perfusion.
row_d
Blood pressure should be monitored every few minutes until stable.
hypotheses: Autonomic dysreflexia triggered by bladder distention
solutions: Immediate response: sit upright and loosen tight clothing
Trigger removal: check catheter tubing, drainage bag, bladder, bowel, and skin
Monitoring: repeat blood pressure every 2 to 5 minutes
Unsafe: lie flat and wait for headache medicine to work
Escalation: use prescribed short-acting antihypertensive if severe hypertension persists
actions: Teach Ethan to sit upright immediately during symptoms
Teach Ethan to check catheter tubing and bladder drainage first
Teach that severe headache with high blood pressure can wait until the next clinic visit
Provide an autonomic dysreflexia emergency wallet card
Teach spouse to call emergency services if symptoms or severe hypertension persist after trigger checks
eval: eval_a
States first action is to sit upright and loosen clothing
eval_b
Identifies blocked catheter or full bladder as a common trigger
eval_c
Says he should lie flat until the headache passes
eval_d
Explains emergency help is needed if blood pressure stays high after trigger removal
